blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have fundamentally transformed the paradigms of
natural language processing, computer vision, and software engineering by
enabling sophisticated text generation, contextual reasoning, and zero-shot
problem-solving [ 1 , 2 ] . At the core of modern LLM
architectures lies the Transformer model, which relies heavily on the
Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mechanism to perform sequence modeling [ 3 ] . This mechanism enables the model to dynamically capture
long-range global dependencies across a sequence, establishing MHA as the
standard for autoregressive language generation and deep context
understanding.

blocks.en:
Despite its unparalleled success, scaling traditional MHA to exceptionally
long contexts remains constrained by its inherent quadratic computational
complexity O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) , where N N denotes the sequence length. As the context
window expands, the memory footprint required to store the Key-Value (KV)
cache grows linearly with context length while the cost of the attention
computation itself grows quadratically, together precipitating a critical
“memory wall” that exhausts available Video RAM (VRAM) [ 4 ] . This
memory problem not only drives up computational infrastructure costs but also
leads to long-context degradation, where the model’s token-processing
efficiency drops significantly, and its retrieval capabilities suffer from
structural information loss deep within lengthy prompts [ 5 ] .

To alleviate this quadratic complexity, alternative sub-quadratic sequence
mixing paradigms have been proposed, including State-Space Models (SSMs),
linear-time recurrent layers, and specialized linear attention approximations [ 6 , 7 ] . Architectures such as Mamba and RWKV compress
the sequence history into a fixed-size latent state, effectively reducing
spatial complexity to O ⁡ ( N ) O(N) during inference. However, these pure recurrent
implementations frequently suffer from sequential processing latency on
parallel hardware during training and can exhibit degraded semantic
understanding. Specifically, they lack the strong global associative recall
capabilities of standard MHA, leading to suboptimal performance on tasks that
require tight, non-local token dependencies.

To address the trade-off between the expressive power of attention and the
computational efficiency of recurrent networks, recent architectural trends
have shifted toward hybrid sequence modeling paradigms [ 8 , 9 ] . Models like Griffin and Jamba interleave
MHA layers with gated linear recurrences or SSMs to achieve sub-quadratic
memory scaling while preserving long-range contextual fidelity. Building on
this paradigm, this paper investigates substituting standard attention with a
Dynamic Wave recurrent layer that leverages exponential damping and phase
modulation to maintain a stable, long-term memory state.

blocks.en: The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
blocks.zh: 本文件的主要贡献如下:

blocks.en:
• The mathematical apparatus of the Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on
input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, is formalized
for sequence processing, and its relationship to complex-valued diagonal state
spaces is made explicit. • The recurrence is shown to be an associative scan, so that it admits the
same O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) -depth parallelization as the state-space layers it is
compared against. • Three comparable 10.94M-parameter architectures (Pure Transformer, Pure
Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) are proposed, implemented, and compared at a
matched parameter budget. • A measurement protocol is introduced that separates mixer memory from
output-layer memory and controls for the attention backend, the compilation
setting, and allocator state; it is shown that omitting these controls
produces qualitatively wrong conclusions. • An implementation-level ablation quantifies how much of the recurrent
layer’s latency penalty is architectural and how much is an artifact of an
unoptimized loop. • A closed-form model of peak activation memory is derived and validated
against measurement; it reproduces the observed figures and predicts the
context length beyond which attention, rather than the vocabulary projection,
dominates memory. • A hardware-aware strategy selection model is developed to guide
architectural choices under explicit operational constraints.

blocks.en: II-A Quadratic Attention and Its Hardware Cost
blocks.zh: II-A 四方关注及其硬件成本

blocks.en:
Multi-Head Attention computes pairwise interactions between every pair of
tokens in a sequence, giving the Transformer its characteristic O ⁡ ( T 2 ⋅ d ) O(T^{2}\!\cdot\!d) time and O ⁡ ( T ⋅ d ) O(T\!\cdot\!d) key-value (KV) cache memory

blocks.en: II-B Sparse and Low-Rank Attention Approximations
blocks.zh: II-B 分层和低倾角注意

blocks.en:
A first family of alternatives keeps the attention mechanism but restricts or
approximates which token pairs interact. Longformer combines a local sliding
window with a small number of global tokens [ 16 ] . Linformer
projects the key and value sequences onto a lower-rank subspace, reducing
complexity to O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) at the cost of a fixed projection length [ 10 ] . Reformer replaces full attention with
locality-sensitive hashing to approximate nearest-neighbor attention [ 17 ] . Performers approximate the softmax kernel with random
feature maps to obtain a linear-time estimator of standard attention [ 11 ] . Ring Attention distributes exact attention across
devices using blockwise computation to scale context length rather than
reducing its asymptotic cost [ 18 ] . These methods remain
attention-shaped: they still model pairwise or approximately pairwise token
interaction, and most require either a specialized kernel or an accuracy
trade-off to realize their theoretical savings.

A second family removes pairwise interaction entirely and replaces it with a
compressed recurrent state. Mamba introduces an input-dependent
(“selective”) state-space model whose transition parameters are computed
from the input at every step, combined with a hardware-aware parallel scan [ 6 ] . RWKV reformulates attention as a linear, RNN-like
recurrence that can be trained in parallel and run in constant memory during
generation [ 7 ] . RetNet introduces an explicit multi-scale
exponential decay (“retention”) term as a direct algebraic substitute for
softmax attention [ 19 ] . Katharopoulos et al. show that linear
attention itself can be reformulated as a recurrent network, unifying the
attention and RNN views [ 20 ] . S4 models long sequences
with a structured, continuous-time state space discretized into a linear
recurrence [ 12 ] ; its diagonal successors S4D [ 21 ] and the
Linear Recurrent Unit [ 22 ] keep a per-channel complex

blocks.en: III-A Design Rationale
blocks.zh: III-A 设计理由

blocks.en:
Retention-based and real-valued state-space layers such as RetNet and Mamba
replace attention with a leaky integrator whose memory decays monotonically
over time [ 6 , 19 ] . Such a kernel can express recency
bias but not constructive or destructive interference between tokens that are
not adjacent, since a purely decaying, non-oscillatory kernel weights every
past token with the same sign. Diagonal state spaces recover oscillation by
moving to complex eigenvalues [ 21 , 22 ] , at the cost of
complex-valued state and arithmetic. The Dynamic Wave layer keeps the state
real and obtains the same qualitative behavior directly: it retains the
exponential damping envelope, so that recent tokens are still weighted more
heavily than distant ones, but modulates the contribution of each incoming
token with a learned, input-dependent cosine term. Each channel of the hidden state therefore behaves like a driven, damped
harmonic oscillator rather than a monotonically decaying accumulator: the sign
and magnitude with which a token enters the running memory depends on a
learned phase, so that subsequent tokens can reinforce or cancel earlier
contributions. Both the damping rate and the oscillation frequency and phase
are computed from the input at every time step, making the recurrence
selective in the same sense as Mamba’s input-dependent transition parameters [ 6 ] , while remaining a much simpler, single-layer recurrence
than a full structured state-space model.

blocks.en: VI-A Dataset and Tokenization
blocks.zh: VI-A 数据集和数据化

blocks.en:
All models are trained on a 500 000-story subset of the TinyStories corpus [ 13 ] , a dataset of short, syntactically simple
children’s stories designed to let small models learn coherent English. A
byte-pair-encoding tokenizer with a 10 000-token vocabulary is trained from
scratch on the same subset using whitespace pre-tokenization. Tokenized
stories are concatenated and split into fixed-length chunks of 512 tokens,
yielding 207 113 training chunks; the last 2000 chunks are held out for
evaluation and are not seen during training. Training batches of 32 chunks are
sampled with shuffling and dropped-last batching, giving 6472 optimization
steps per epoch.

blocks.en: VII-B Qualitative Generation Behavior
blocks.zh: VII-B 定性生成行为

blocks.en:
For the prompt “Once upon a time, a little boy named Tom went to the forest
and found a”, all three models produce fluent, on-topic continuations under
greedy decoding. The Transformer continues with “a big tree”, which Tom
climbs; the Hybrid model produces a similar but independently-phrased
continuation about climbing a tree; Pure Wave instead introduces a different
object (“a big, shiny rock”) and a different narrative arc, demonstrating
that Pure Wave is not simply imitating the Transformer’s output distribution.
On a second, longer prompt designed to probe entity tracking over a longer
span, the Transformer and Hybrid models both continue coherently and keep
referring to the already-introduced characters, while Pure Wave’s continuation
introduces an ungrounded new character not present in the prompt—a mild form
of entity drift consistent with the weaker associative-recall behavior
reported for linear-time sequence models in general [ 27 ] . A
temperature- and noise-robustness stress test on the Hybrid model
(temperature 0.2, 1.5, and 10% random-token corruption of the prompt) shows
graceful degradation in every case.

(forward and backward) at 512 tokens with batch size 8. The ranking inverts

fused attention baseline Pure Wave is the most expensive of the three
configurations, at 621.2 MB against 573.6 MB, 8.3% more. The reason is that
the Wave recurrence must retain every intermediate state h t h_{t} for the
backward pass—an O ⁡ ( T ⋅ d ) O(T\!\cdot\!d) autograd tape with T T separate nodes—whereas
a fused attention kernel recomputes its intermediates and stores comparatively
little. A recurrent mixer that is cheaper at inference time is therefore not
automatically cheaper to train.

blocks.en: VIII-A Hybridization Improves Quality, and Is Neutral for Peak Memory

blocks.en:
The Hybrid configuration delivers the best language-modeling quality of the
three (14.1% lower perplexity than the Transformer baseline,
Section VII-A ) and the best qualitative entity-tracking
behavior (Section VII-B ), supporting the hypothesis that
placing cheap sequential compression before global attention, as in Griffin
and Jamba [ 8 , 9 ] , is an effective design pattern
at this scale. On peak memory, however, it is indistinguishable from the Pure
Transformer under both attention backends
(Section VII-E ). Peak memory is determined by the largest
single allocation in the forward pass, so replacing half of the attention
layers leaves that maximum untouched. A hybrid design should therefore be
justified on the quality axis; on the peak-memory axis it is neither a gain
nor a loss, and its benefit appears only in aggregate quantities such as
KV-cache size during incremental decoding.

blocks.en: VIII-E Limitations
blocks.zh: VIII-E 限制

blocks.en:
Several scope limitations qualify the conclusions above. First, all models are
trained for a single epoch, at a single scale (10.94M parameters), on a single,
syntactically simple dataset [ 13 ] ; whether the
perplexity ranking observed here holds at larger scale, over multiple training
seeds, or on more complex, long-document corpora such as The Pile [ 38 ] is not established. Second, the training wall-clock comparison of
Section VII-I and the generation-throughput comparison of
Section VII-H remain confounded by the torch.compile asymmetry, since both were measured with a compiled baseline against
uncompiled recurrent configurations; only the memory and forward-latency
benchmarks are compile-free for all three. Third, no
incremental, state-caching decoding path is implemented, so the
generation-throughput results measure the current reference implementation
rather than the recurrence’s ceiling. Fourth, the interpretability analysis
uses a single example sentence and is illustrative rather than systematic;
broader protocols such as HELM [ 44 ] would be a natural
extension. Fifth, the comparison includes no established sub-quadratic
baseline: benchmarking the Dynamic Wave layer against Mamba [ 6 ] , RWKV [ 7 ] and linear attention [ 20 ] at a matched parameter budget is required before any
claim of relative merit within the recurrent family can be made, and a
targeted associative-recall benchmark in the style of Zoology [ 27 ] would test directly the recall behavior that
Section VII-B only illustrates. Sixth, all profiling is
performed in FP32 on a single GPU architecture; mixed-precision and
multi-device behavior may differ, particularly for the attention backends,
whose relative cost depends strongly on kernel availability.

Based on the results of Section VII , the following guidance is
proposed for choosing among the three configurations, rather than treating one
architecture as universally superior.

blocks.en: X Conclusions
blocks.zh: 十. 结论

blocks.en:
This paper formalized a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on
input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, as an
alternative and a complement to standard Multi-Head Attention, and evaluated
three 10.94M-parameter configurations under a measurement protocol that
isolates each configuration, separates mixer memory from output-layer memory,
and names the attention backend for every figure.
blocks.zh:
本文根据
依赖输入的指数式起坝和余弦相调制,作为一种
对标准多头关注的替代和补充
测量协议下的三个10.94M参数配置
隔离每个配置,将混音器内存与输出层内存分离,
并指定每个图的注意后端。

blocks.en:
On quality, the results are clear and favorable: the Hybrid Wave-Attention
configuration achieves a perplexity of 5.95 on the full held-out split against
6.93 for the Transformer baseline and 7.26 for Pure Wave, and its peak memory
matches the Transformer to within 0.1%, so this quality gain costs nothing
in that dimension.
blocks.zh:
在质量方面,结果是明确和有利的:混合波-注意
配置实现5.95的迷惑度,与完全搁置的平分
变形器基线6.93和纯波7.26及其峰值内存
将变压器匹配到 0.1% 以内, 因此质量不会增加成本
在这个层面。

blocks.en:
On efficiency, the results are conditional in a way that the framing of much
of the sub-quadratic literature obscures. Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM
than attention at a 4096-token context when attention is computed without a
fused kernel, and exactly as much when it is; in training mode it is 8.3%
more expensive. Similarly, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence
loop sped the layer up 2.53-fold without any custom kernel, reducing its
latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. Neither of the two
efficiency effects usually attributed to the recurrent architecture survives a
controlled measurement: the memory advantage belongs to the attention
baseline’s implementation, and most of the latency penalty to the Wave layer’s
own.

blocks.en:
The broader conclusion is methodological. Efficiency claims for attention
replacements should state the attention backend, the compilation setting, the
allocator protocol, and whether the output layer is included, because in this
study such choices changed headline numbers by factors of two or more and, in
two cases, reversed the ordering they implied. The recurrence studied here is an associative scan
(Section III-C ), so the parallel form is available in principle;
what is missing is an implementation of it. Future work should supply that
kernel together with a state-caching decoding path, disentangle the torch.compile asymmetry, benchmark the Dynamic Wave layer against
Mamba [ 6 ] , RWKV [ 7 ] and linear attention [ 20 ] at a matched budget, and extend the evaluation to
larger models, multiple seeds, targeted associative-recall tests, and longer
corpora such as The Pile [ 38 ] .
